blocks.text: Lesson 9 — Cloud security, IAM and configuration hygiene

LEARNING OUTCOME
Secure cloud identities, network boundaries, storage policies, audit trails and configuration changes.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Cloud providers secure parts of the underlying platform, while customers retain responsibilities for identities, data, configuration, workloads and applications. Exact responsibilities depend on the service model. Write down each control owner and alert recipient.

blocks.text: Use MFA, role-based access, short-lived credentials, scoped service identities and separation of development and production. Review public exposure, inbound rules, storage access, encryption settings and backups. Prefer reviewed infrastructure-as-code and automated policy checks over undocumented console changes.

blocks.text: Small changes can expose storage or grant excessive privileges. Log administrative changes, alert on high-impact drift, use approved templates and test incident and restore procedures. Use fabricated secrets and data in lessons; never paste real production keys into tutorial code.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.question: What is cloud shared responsibility?
options: The provider handles every customer setting
Provider and customer have different security duties based on the service
blocks.explanation: Responsibilities vary by service model; document who owns each control.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: How can a team detect dangerous configuration drift?
options: Audit changes and alert on high-impact settings
blocks.explanation: Audit and policy checks help detect unexpected exposure and privilege changes.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which approach better protects private information?
options: Use synthetic data and collect only necessary, authorized evidence
Copy all customer records for convenience
blocks.explanation: Data minimization and redaction reduce privacy and exposure risks.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
